flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{1-\cos mx}{x^{2}}=\frac{m^{2}}{2}$$Write 1 minus cosine mx as twice the sine squared of mx over 2, divide by x squared, and the coefficient shortcut gives twice m over 2, all squared, which is m squared over 2.

flashcards.q: What is the limit of (tangent x minus sine x) over x cubed as x tends to 0, and how do you get it?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\tan x-\sin x}{x^{3}}=\frac{1}{2}$$One half. Write tangent as sine over cosine, take sine x out, replace 1 minus cosine x by twice the sine squared of the half angle, and divide by x cubed. It is the most frequently asked trigonometric limit in the chapter.

flashcards.q: What is sine of infinity, and how do you handle the limit of 2 to the x, times sine of 2 to the minus x, as x tends to infinity?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to \infty} 2^{x}\sin\!\left(2^{-x}\right) = 1$$Sine of infinity is a bounded oscillating value somewhere between minus 1 and 1, with no fixed value. The limit is a 0 times infinity form: send the 2 to the x into the denominator so the inner quantity goes to 0, and the limit is 1.

flashcards.q: Is sine x over x equal to 1 as x tends to pi over 2?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to \pi/2} \frac{\sin x}{x} = \frac{2}{\pi}$$No. Sine x over x goes to 1 only as x tends to 0. At pi over 2 there is no indeterminate form at all, so you substitute, and the value is 2 over pi.

flashcards.q: Nothing manipulates nicely and the limit is at x tending to a. What is the universal escape?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to a} f(x) \text{ exists} \iff \lim_{h \to 0} f(a+h) = \lim_{h \to 0} f(a-h)$$Substitute x equal to a plus h, or a minus h, so that h tends to 0 and every standard formula applies again. Those two substitutions are the right-hand and left-hand limits, and the substitution must be made in the whole expression at once, never in selected pieces.

flashcards.q: The greatest integer of sine 2x over x, and of tangent 5x over x, as x tends to 0. Why do they differ in style?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to 0} \left[\frac{\sin x}{x}\right] = 0, \qquad \lim_{x \to 0} \left[\frac{\tan x}{x}\right] = 1$$Sine t over t comes up to 1 from below and tangent t over t comes down to 1 from above. So sine 2x over x sits just below 2 and its greatest integer is 1, while tangent 5x over x sits just above 5 and its greatest integer is 5.

flashcards.q: State the logarithmic limit, and say what you do when the log does not show a 1.
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{u \to 0} \frac{\ln(1+u)}{u} = 1$$Log of 1 plus something, over that same something, goes to 1 when the something goes to 0. If the 1 is missing, add and subtract 1 inside the log, or take the constant out and split it with the log of a product.

flashcards.q: Why can you not split the limit of log(1 plus 2h) over h squared, minus twice log(1 plus h) over h squared, as h tends to 0?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{h \to 0}\left[\frac{\ln(1+2h)}{h^{2}} - \frac{2\ln(1+h)}{h^{2}}\right]$$Each piece is a finite quantity over h, which is infinite, so splitting creates an infinity minus infinity form and the apparent answer 0 is wrong. Merge the logs first and the limit is minus 1.

flashcards.q: State the exponential limits, including the version with a general base.
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{a^x - 1}{x} = \ln a$$a to the x, minus 1, over x, goes to log a; and e to the something, minus 1, over that same something, goes to 1 when the something goes to 0. For a to the x minus b to the x, over x, take b to the x common to manufacture the 1, giving log of a over b.

flashcards.q: Evaluate the limit as x tends to 0 of (e to the cosine 2x, minus e) over tangent squared 3x.
flashcards.a: $$\cos 2x - 1 = -2\sin^{2} x$$Take e common to get e times (e to the cosine 2x minus 1, minus 1) over tangent squared 3x. The exponential block over cosine 2x minus 1 tends to 1, and cosine 2x minus 1 is minus twice sine squared x, so the value is minus 2e over 9.

flashcards.q: Give the complete method for a 1 to the power infinity limit.
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x\to a} f(x)^{g(x)} = e^{\lambda}, \quad \lambda = \lim_{x\to a}\big(f(x)-1\big)\,g(x)$$Check that the base goes to 1 and the power goes to infinity. Compute lambda as the limit of base minus 1, times the power, which is a 0 times infinity form handled by bringing the power down. The answer is e to the lambda, never lambda.

flashcards.q: Which expansions must you have by heart, and what is the one that catches people out?
flashcards.a: $$(1+x)^{n} = 1 + nx + \frac{n(n-1)}{2!}x^{2} + \frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{3!}x^{3} + \cdots$$Sine, cosine, tangent, e to the x, log of 1 plus x, and the binomial. Tangent is the trap: its denominators are plain 3 and 15, not factorials, and the series is only valid between minus pi over 2 and pi over 2.

flashcards.q: What single observation solves nearly every expansion limit?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{a x^{m} + \cdots}{\alpha x^{n} + \cdots} = \begin{cases} a/\alpha & m = n \\ 0 & m > n \\ \text{undefined} & m < n \end{cases}$$For a finite non-zero limit, the minimum power of x in the numerator equals the minimum power in the denominator, and the limit is the ratio of those two coefficients. Every higher power is irrelevant.

flashcards.q: The denominator is x squared and the numerator is a bracket raised to a fractional power, with the lower terms already cancelled. What is the answer?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{(1+2x)^{1/3}-1-\frac{2x}{3}}{x^{2}} = \frac{\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{1}{3}-1\right)}{2!}\cdot 2^{2} = -\frac{4}{9}$$One coefficient: the index term n times n minus 1, over 2 factorial, multiplied by the square of the coefficient of x inside the bracket. For the cube root of 1 plus 2x, minus 1, minus two thirds x, over x squared, that gives minus 4 over 9.

flashcards.q: State the test for continuity of f at x = a, in the form you check it.
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = f(a)$$Left limit equals right limit equals f(a), all three finite. The left limit comes from the definition just below a, the right limit from the definition just above a, and f(a) by plain substitution.

flashcards.q: Find the left and right limits of (e to the 1 over x, minus 1) over (e to the 1 over x, plus 1) at x = 0.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{e^{1/x}-1}{e^{1/x}+1} = \frac{1 - \dfrac{1}{e^{1/x}}}{1 + \dfrac{1}{e^{1/x}}}$$From the left, 1 over x runs to minus infinity and the exponential dies, so the limit is minus 1. From the right the form is infinity over infinity, so divide top and bottom by the exponential to get 1. A jump of 2, so the discontinuity at 0 is irremovable.

flashcards.q: Distinguish removable from irremovable discontinuity, and name the sub-cases.
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to a} f(x) \text{ exists, but } \lim_{x \to a} f(x) \neq f(a)$$Removable means the limit exists but does not equal f(a), so one redefinition repairs it: isolated point when f(a) is given and different, missing point when f(a) is not given at all. Irremovable means the limit does not exist: a jump when the one-sided limits are finite but unequal, oscillating when a one-sided limit does not exist.

flashcards.q: A greatest-integer continuity question is set on a quadratic. What is the actual work?
flashcards.a: $$[x] = n \quad \text{for } n \le x < n+1$$Graph the quadratic on the given interval from its vertex and its end values, read off which integer levels the curve crosses, and solve the quadratic equal to each of those integers. Those x values are the breaks, so it is a range question rather than a continuity question. Say in the working whether the end points of the interval are being counted, because the published key counts them and a reading that takes interior points only gives a different total.

flashcards.q: How do you test the continuity of f(g(x)) at x = a without ever building the composite?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x\to a^+} f(g(x)) = f\!\left(g(a^+)\right), \qquad \lim_{x\to a^-} f(g(x)) = f\!\left(g(a^-)\right)$$Find the three limiting values of g at a, from the left, from the right and at the point itself, keeping track of whether each sits slightly above or below its value. Feed those three into f and compare. Then add separately any point where g itself is undefined.

flashcards.q: For f(x) = (x plus 1) over (x minus 1) and g(x) = 1 over (x minus 2), where is f(g(x)) discontinuous?
flashcards.a: $$f(x) = \frac{x+1}{x-1},\quad g(x) = \frac{1}{x-2} \;\Rightarrow\; (f \circ g)(x) = \frac{x-1}{3-x}$$Simplifying gives x minus 1, over 3 minus x, which breaks at x = 3. But x = 2 must be added, because g itself blows up there and the cancellation that produced the simplified form is meaningless at that point. So x = 2 and x = 3.

flashcards.q: What does the derivative at a point mean geometrically, and what are the right and left hand derivatives?
flashcards.a: $$f'(a^{-}) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a-h) - f(a)}{-h}, \quad h > 0$$It is the slope of the tangent: the chord through the point and its neighbour becomes the tangent as the gap closes. The right hand derivative uses plus h over h, and the left hand derivative uses minus h over minus h, with h positive in both.

flashcards.q: State the two conditions for differentiability at x = a, and the one-line reason.
flashcards.a: $$f \text{ differentiable at } x=a \iff f \text{ continuous at } x=a \ \text{ and } \ f'(a^{+}) = f'(a^{-})$$The function must be continuous at a, and the right hand derivative must equal the left hand derivative. Both say the same thing geometrically: exactly one tangent can be drawn at the point.

flashcards.q: The two one-sided derivatives come out equal, but the function jumps at that point. Is it differentiable?
flashcards.a: $$f'(a^{+}) = f'(a^{-})$$No. A discontinuous function is non-differentiable there, whatever the two derivatives turn out to be, because two different tangents exist. Always check continuity before spending time on derivatives.

flashcards.q: What is the working shortcut for the differentiability of a piecewise function?
flashcards.a: $$f'(a^{+}) = \left[\frac{d}{dx}\,f_{\,x>a}(x)\right]_{x=a}$$Differentiate each piece separately, then substitute the point into each derivative. That gives the right hand derivative from the upper branch and the left hand derivative from the lower branch, without writing out the first-principles limits.

flashcards.q: You are handed a modulus function and asked about differentiability. What is the first line, and what does it tell you?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dx}|x - a| = \begin{cases} +1, & x > a \\ -1, & x < a \end{cases}$$Split the modulus at the point where the inside becomes zero, which turns it into an ordinary piecewise function. The slope is plus one on the right and minus one on the left, so the function is continuous but not differentiable at that point.

flashcards.q: For f(x) = (x minus 2) times the modulus of x squared minus 4, where is it differentiable, and why the asymmetry?
flashcards.a: $$f'(x) = (x-2)^2 + 2(x+2)(x-2) = (x-2)(3x+2)$$Differentiable at x = 2 but not at x = minus 2. Near 2 the function carries a repeated factor of x minus 2, which flattens the corner, so both one-sided derivatives are 0. At minus 2 the two one-sided derivatives are plus 16 and minus 16.

flashcards.q: For f(x) = x squared times the greatest integer of x, discuss x = 0 and x = 2.
flashcards.a: $$\lfloor x \rfloor = n \quad \text{for } n \le x < n+1$$At 0 the branches are 0 for x at or above 0 and minus x squared below, so both the value and both derivatives are 0: continuous and differentiable. At 2 the branches are twice x squared and x squared, the value jumps from 4 to 8, so the function is discontinuous and non-differentiable, and the derivatives 8 and 4 are irrelevant.

flashcards.q: f is continuous at a and g is discontinuous at a. What can you say about f plus g and about f times g?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \lim_{x \to a^{-}} f(x)g(x) = 0 = \lim_{x \to a^{+}} f(x)g(x)$$The sum and the difference are certainly discontinuous. The product need not be: if the limit of f at a is 0, the product can still be continuous. If both f and g are discontinuous, nothing can be said about the sum, difference or product.

flashcards.q: f is differentiable with f dashed at 5 equal to 7. Evaluate the limit as t tends to 0 of f(5 plus t) minus f(5 minus t), all over 2t.
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dt}\,f(5-t) = -f'(5-t)$$By L'Hôpital in t, the derivative of f(5 minus t) carries a factor of minus one, so the two terms add: the limit is f dashed at 5, which is 7, not 0.

flashcards.q: Why is x squared times sine of 1 over x differentiable at 0, while x times sine of 1 over x is not?
flashcards.a: $$f'(a^{+}) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}$$By first principles the first gives h times sine of 1 over h, which is 0 because the sine stays bounded. For the second the quotient is sine of 1 over h, which oscillates and has no limit. Direct differentiation fails in both cases, which is exactly when you must return to the definition.

flashcards.q: When does a two-sided limit exist at all?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L \iff \lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = L$$Only when the left hand limit and the right hand limit both exist and agree. Their common value is the limit — putting 9.9999 and 10.0001 into the function is only imitating that check.

flashcards.q: In a 0/0 limit, what exactly are you cancelling?
flashcards.a: Not a zero. You cancel the identical non-zero quantity, the x minus 3 that is approaching 0 on the top and on the bottom. If zeros could cancel, 0 equals 0 times 5 and 0 equals 0 times 7 would make 5 equal 7.

flashcards.q: Which identity removes a surd from a 0/0 limit, and how is it used?
flashcards.a: $$(a-b)(a+b)=a^2-b^2$$The difference of two squares. Multiply the surd expression by its conjugate, so the roots get squared away and the common factor appears.

flashcards.q: Roots on the top and on the bottom — how many conjugates, and in how many lines?
flashcards.a: Count the root terms before starting. A root on top only needs one conjugate; roots above and below need both conjugates, multiplied in the same line. Done as two separate attempts, a factor gets lost.

flashcards.q: The denominator of a limit vanishes and the limit is a finite number. What is forced?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = L \ (\text{finite}),\ g(x) \to 0 \ \Rightarrow \ f(x) \to 0$$The numerator must go to 0 as well. A non-zero constant over a vanishing quantity is infinite, not finite, so this is the first equation you write — for free, before any algebra.

flashcards.q: Two unknowns, and only the zero-numerator condition written down. Where does the second equation come from?
flashcards.a: From the given limit value itself. Cancel the common factor, substitute, and set what is left equal to the value you were given.

flashcards.q: What is the single rule that every 0/0 question obeys?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = L \;\text{with}\; f(c)=g(c)=0 \;\Rightarrow\; \text{cancel } (x-c) \text{ first, then put } x=c$$Kill the common factor first, and substitute only after it is gone. Substituting at the start gives 0 equals 0, which is true for every value of the unknown and tells you nothing.

flashcards.q: How does the practice pair prove that 0/0 has no fixed value?
flashcards.a: The same 0/0 form comes out as 5 once a is pinned at 24. So the symbol carries no value of its own — it is a signal to simplify, never an answer.

flashcards.q: Which single fact makes the divide-by-the-highest-power method work?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{c}{x^{n}} = 0, \quad n > 0$$Any fixed number over a positive power of x dies to 0 as x runs to infinity. It does not matter whether the power is 2, a half or four thirds.

flashcards.q: Why not simply memorise the ratio of the leading coefficients?
flashcards.a: Because it is only the result of the division, and carrying it as a memorised shortcut is how the minus sign gets dropped in a case like 7 over minus 2.

flashcards.q: After dividing by a base raised to x, how do you know you picked the right base?
flashcards.a: Glance at each leftover base. Below 1, such as two thirds, the term is 0. Above 1, such as three halves, it blows up — which means you divided by the smaller base and must go back and divide by the larger one.

flashcards.q: The top settles at a non-zero number and the bottom creeps to 0. Which infinity is the answer?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{3x^{3}-7}{-2x^{2}+5}=\lim_{x\to\infty}\frac{3-\frac{7}{x^{3}}}{-\frac{2}{x}+\frac{5}{x^{3}}}=\frac{3}{0^{-}}=-\infty$$Read the sign of the surviving bottom term: 0 from above gives plus infinity, 0 from below gives minus infinity. With minus 2 over x surviving underneath, the limit is minus infinity.

flashcards.q: Should you memorise a separate rule for unequal powers?
flashcards.a: No. Divide by the highest power of x you can see and the answer declares itself as 0 or as an infinity. The rule about which degree is bigger is a consequence of that division, not an extra tool to remember the wrong way round.

flashcards.q: For a ratio of polynomials as x runs to infinity, what are the three possible outcomes?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{a_m x^m + \cdots}{b_n x^n + \cdots} = \frac{a_m}{b_n} \ \text{if } m = n, \quad 0 \ \text{if } m < n, \quad \infty \ \text{if } m > n$$Equal degrees give the ratio of the leading coefficients; a bigger degree below gives 0; a bigger degree above gives an infinite limit.

flashcards.q: Is 3 over 0 an acceptable final answer to an infinity over infinity limit?
flashcards.a: No. That line is your reasoning, not an answer. Write that the limit tends to infinity, which means no finite limit exists.

flashcards.q: Cubic over cubic, already in brackets. What is the value and how quickly can you see it?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{n(n+1)(2n+1)}{(n^{2}+2)(-3n+5)} = -\frac{2}{3}$$Equal degrees, so the limit is the ratio of the leading coefficients: 2 over minus 3, that is minus two thirds. The answer can be written before the solution is.

flashcards.q: Why not expand the brackets before dividing?
flashcards.a: The answer is the same but two minutes are gone and a sign slip invited. Count the degrees on the factored form and hand out the powers of n inside the brackets, checking that they multiply back to the same power above and below.

flashcards.q: What happens inside a square root when you divide it by x?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{1}{x}\sqrt{A} = \sqrt{\frac{A}{x^2}} \quad (x > 0)$$Every term inside gets divided by x squared, because a factor crossing into a root is squared. Pushing 2 inside root 5 gives root of 2 squared times 5, and the same thing happens in reverse.

flashcards.q: The root contains x squared. Why divide by x rather than by x squared?
flashcards.a: The root halves the power, so the whole expression behaves like degree one. Judge the power after the root, never before it — dividing by x squared collapses the limit to 0 wrongly.

flashcards.q: On the negative side of the number line, what is the square root of x squared?
flashcards.a: $$\sqrt{x^{2}} = |x| = -x \quad (x < 0)$$The modulus of x, which is minus x when x is negative. That is exactly where a direct division by x flips the sign and loses the mark.

flashcards.q: After substituting x equal to minus t, what else has to change?
flashcards.a: The limit itself: t runs to plus infinity. And squared terms keep their sign, since minus t all squared is t squared; only the odd-power and plain x terms pick up the minus.

flashcards.q: What two conditions make this expression have a finite limit?
flashcards.a: $$1-a=0,\qquad b-a=L$$Kill the coefficient of x squared, which fixes a, and then match the coefficient of x to the given limit. Those are the only two lines you need.

flashcards.q: Why take the LCM instead of dividing by the highest power straight away?
flashcards.a: Because the form is infinity minus infinity, not infinity over infinity — there is no single fraction yet. Build the fraction with the LCM first, then divide.

flashcards.q: After taking the LCM, which coefficient do you read first?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{x^{2}+1}{x+1}-ax+b=\frac{(1-a)x^{2}+(b-a)x+(1+b)}{x+1}$$The x squared coefficient, set to zero — that gives a. Only then read the x coefficient and set it equal to the given limit to get b.

flashcards.q: What goes wrong if you use the given limit value before clearing the x squared term?
flashcards.a: Nothing is salvageable: while the x squared coefficient is non-zero the limit does not exist at all. Set it to zero first, get a, and only then use the value you were given.

flashcards.q: How do you handle shifted powers such as 3 to the power n plus 1?
flashcards.a: Treat them as coefficients in disguise: 3 to the power n plus 1 is 3 times 3 to the n, 2 to the power n plus 2 is 4 times 2 to the n, and 2 to the power n minus 1 is half of 2 to the n. Write that line and the question becomes one you have already solved.

flashcards.q: Does n have to be a whole number in the algebraic limit formula?
flashcards.a: No. It can be a fraction or negative and n times a to the power n minus 1 still holds. What must match is the power on both terms and the constant x is tending to.

flashcards.q: State the rule for differentiating a limit, and the check that comes before it.
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}$$Substitute first: only a 0/0 or an infinity over infinity form lets you differentiate the top alone and the bottom alone, then substitute again. Repeat until a finite number appears; any other value at the start is already the answer.

flashcards.q: Which rule must never appear inside one of these differentiation steps?
flashcards.a: The quotient rule. The moment a square turns up in the denominator you have differentiated the whole fraction instead of the two parts — stop and restart with top alone, bottom alone.

flashcards.q: Which sum formula finishes the x plus x squared up to x to the n, minus n, question?
flashcards.a: $$1+2+3+\cdots+n=\frac{n(n+1)}{2}$$The sum of the first n natural numbers, n times n plus 1 over 2. After differentiating, every power of 1 is 1, so the coefficients simply add up.

flashcards.q: In a limit as x approaches a, how is a term built only from a treated?
flashcards.a: As a constant, so its derivative is 0. Differentiate with respect to x only, and substitute x equal to a at the end.

flashcards.q: Before writing 1 for a sine-over-something limit, what two things must be checked?
flashcards.a: That the expression inside the sine is identical to the one in the denominator, and that this expression itself approaches 0. If it does not become 0 there is no indeterminate form and you simply substitute.

flashcards.q: At x approaching pi over 2, how is a cosine limit turned into a sine limit?
flashcards.a: $$\cos x = \sin\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - x\right)$$Write cosine x as the sine of pi over 2 minus x. The angle inside the sine now goes to 0, and the denominator can be matched to that angle.

flashcards.q: The form is 0/0 but the angle inside the sine approaches pi. What then?
flashcards.a: The 0/0 form alone is not enough — the angle itself must approach 0, so rewrite sine x as the sine of pi minus x. Whatever constant you pull out while matching the denominator stays in the answer.

flashcards.q: Why is sine ax over x not simply 1?
flashcards.a: Because the value 1 needs the angle and the denominator to be the exact same quantity. Here the angle is ax and the bottom is x, so the limit is a — and if you push an a into the denominator you must push the same a onto the top.

flashcards.q: What is the limit of sine cubed of 2x over x cubed as x approaches 0?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin^{3} 2x}{x^{3}} = \left(\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin 2x}{x}\right)^{3} = 2^{3} = 8$$Take the limit of one bracket, sine 2x over x, which is 2, and then apply the power. The answer is 2 cubed, that is 8.

flashcards.q: A 0/0 limit built only from sines and tangents over powers of x — what is the move?
flashcards.a: Divide the numerator and the denominator by x and every term becomes its own coefficient. Nothing needs expanding, and no sign changes: a minus in the question stays a minus in the answer.

flashcards.q: Why avoid cosine squared x minus sine squared x inside a limit?
flashcards.a: Those forms are fine in trigonometry but useless here. Choose the form that leaves a pure sine, so that sine of something over that same something can be used.

flashcards.q: When is a limit allowed to split across a product?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x\to a}\big(f(x)\cdot g(x)\big)=\lim_{x\to a}f(x)\cdot\lim_{x\to a}g(x)$$Only once each piece has a limit that exists and is finite. Remove the indeterminate form first, by dividing by x or by factoring, and only then take limits piece by piece.

flashcards.q: Sine of x minus 3, over x squared minus 9. Why is this not 1?
flashcards.a: The denominator has to be the same expression as the one inside the sine. Factor out x minus 3 first and keep 1 over x plus 3 aside as an ordinary factor.

flashcards.q: Where does the halving in these 1 minus cosine answers come from?
flashcards.a: From the identity: 1 minus cosine of an angle is twice the sine squared of half that angle. So the coefficient inside the sine is halved, and because the sine is squared that halved coefficient is squared too.

flashcards.q: A degree sign appears inside a limit. What is the first move?
flashcards.a: $$x^{\circ} = x \times \frac{\pi}{180} \ \text{radian}$$Convert to radians by multiplying the angle by pi over 180, before any limit formula is applied. Then the new coefficient of x is the answer.

flashcards.q: Why is the limit of 1 minus cosine 4x over x squared equal to 8 and not 32?
flashcards.a: Because the angle inside the sine is halved: 1 minus cosine 4x is twice the sine squared of 2x. Square the coefficient of x and halve it.

flashcards.q: What is the limit of sine ax over tangent bx as x approaches 0?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin ax}{\tan bx} = \frac{a}{b}$$a over b. Divide the top and the bottom by x and each term turns into its own coefficient.

flashcards.q: A plain tangent x in the denominator — what coefficient does it carry?
flashcards.a: 1, so the whole term reads as 1. That is the piece that turns 5 minus 3 into the answer 2 in the mixed practice set.

flashcards.q: What does dividing every term by x do to a sine ax term?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\sin ax}{x} = a$$It leaves just a, the coefficient of the angle. Once every term has been treated that way, the answer is only the numbers added or subtracted.

flashcards.q: Can the sine be cancelled in sine 5x over sine x?
flashcards.a: No — a sine is not a multiplier. Divide both parts by x and use sine 5x over x going to 5 and sine x over x going to 1 separately.

flashcards.q: The same quantity sits inside the sine and underneath it, and it runs to infinity. What is the limit?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\sin(2^x)}{2^x} = 0$$0. A bounded numerator over a quantity blowing up collapses to 0. The sine-over-the-same-something result needs that something to approach 0, which is not what is happening here.

flashcards.q: How is a 0 times infinity form handled?
flashcards.a: Never leave it as it stands. Send the factor going to infinity into the denominator, where it becomes a quantity going to 0, and you are left with a clean 0/0 that the standard limits can finish.

flashcards.q: A sine or cosine sitting on top of x as x runs to infinity — what is the limit?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\text{bounded}}{x} = 0$$0. A finite oscillating value between minus 1 and plus 1, divided by something blowing up, collapses to 0.

flashcards.q: Two look-alikes at infinity: sine x over x, and x times sine of 1 over x. Why do they land on different answers?
flashcards.a: The first is a bounded value over infinity, so it is 0. The second is a 0 times infinity form: flip the x into the denominator and it reads as sine of 1 over x, divided by 1 over x, where the angle really does approach 0, so the answer is 1.

flashcards.q: Which identity do you reach for when sine squared x minus sine squared y sits on top?
flashcards.a: $$\sin(A+B)\,\sin(A-B) = \sin^2 A - \sin^2 B$$Write it as the sine of the sum times the sine of the difference, so that a difference factor appears and cancels with the denominator.

flashcards.q: After the identity has split the expression, how do you finish?
flashcards.a: Judge each bracket on its own. One bracket may be the 0/0 type worth 1, while the other is just a number once the value is substituted.

flashcards.q: State the identity for a difference of two sines.
flashcards.a: $$\sin C - \sin D = 2\cos\frac{C+D}{2}\,\sin\frac{C-D}{2}$$Twice the cosine of the half sum, times the sine of the half difference. The cosine carries the sum here — unlike the difference of two cosines, where both factors are sines.

flashcards.q: Why bother with the side identities at all?
flashcards.a: Fewer questions is not no questions, and the aim is the same for all of them: turn a difference into a product of sines, so each sine pairs with an x to give 1 and any leftover cosine simply takes its value at 0.

flashcards.q: Is a plain cosine x in a limit at 0 a problem?
flashcards.a: No. At 0 it is simply 1, so stop staring at it. The piece creating the 0/0 is the 1 minus cosine x, and that has one fixed cure: twice the sine squared of half the angle.

flashcards.q: Expand the tangent of a double angle.
flashcards.a: $$\tan 2\theta = \frac{2\tan\theta}{1-\tan^2\theta}$$Twice the tangent of the single angle, over 1 minus the tangent squared of it. The sign below is minus — with a plus it would be the sine of the double angle instead.

flashcards.q: The denominator holds 1 minus cosine 2x, all squared. What is easy to lose?
flashcards.a: The constant. Twice the sine squared of x, all squared, is 4 times the sine to the fourth of x. Dropping that 4 turns the answer from 1 over 2 into 2.

flashcards.q: How is a sine x plus b cosine x compressed into a single sine?
flashcards.a: $$a\sin x + b\cos x = \sqrt{a^2+b^2}\,\left[\frac{a}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}\sin x + \frac{b}{\sqrt{a^2+b^2}}\cos x\right]$$Multiply and divide by the root of a squared plus b squared. The two coefficients left inside become a cosine and a sine of one angle, so the pair compresses into one sine, and the constant pulled outside is the answer here.

flashcards.q: The top has become a sine of pi over 2 minus x, but the denominator still reads pi minus 2x. What now?
flashcards.a: They must be the same bracket, so take 2 common: pi minus 2x is twice pi over 2 minus x. Squaring that 2 outside is exactly where the half in the answer comes from.

flashcards.q: The options include limit does not exist. What has to be computed?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to a} f(x) \text{ exists} \iff \lim_{h \to 0} f(a+h) = \lim_{h \to 0} f(a-h)$$Both one-sided limits: substitute a plus h and then a minus h, with h going to 0 each time. Equal values mean the limit exists, different values mean it does not.

flashcards.q: Which of a plus h and a minus h is the right-hand limit, and what else changes?
flashcards.a: a plus h is the bigger side, so it is the right-hand limit; a minus h is the left-hand one. And the moment you substitute, the whole line must be rewritten with h going to 0, in every term.

flashcards.q: Which allied-angle conversion flips sign between the two sides of this substitution?
flashcards.a: $$\sin(\pi - 2h) = \sin 2h,\quad \sin(\pi + 2h) = -\sin 2h$$The sine of pi minus twice h stays as the sine of twice h, but the sine of pi plus twice h is minus the sine of twice h. Convert the allied angle on every single line.

flashcards.q: The powers on top and bottom do not match. What is the honest step?
flashcards.a: Divide the top and the bottom by h once, pull out each sine-over-its-own-angle as its own number, and keep whatever sine is left over. Here that leftover sine is what drives the answer to 0.

flashcards.q: With the greatest integer inside the limit, what do the sine and tangent ratios give at 0?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to 0} \left[\frac{\sin x}{x}\right] = 0, \qquad \lim_{x \to 0} \left[\frac{\tan x}{x}\right] = 1$$0 and 1. The bracket acts on the value the function actually holds near 0 — just below 1 for the sine ratio, and just above 1 for the tangent ratio.

flashcards.q: Which of the two ratios sits above 1 near 0, and why?
flashcards.a: The tangent one. Near 0 the sine curve lies below the line y equals x while the tangent curve lies above it, so sine x is less than x is less than tangent x.

flashcards.q: What is the greatest integer of x over tangent x as x approaches 0?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to 0}\left[\frac{x}{\tan x}\right] = 0$$0. The tangent ratio sits just above 1, so its reciprocal sits just below 1, and flooring something just below 1 gives 0.

flashcards.q: What does taking a reciprocal do to which side of 1 a ratio sits on?
flashcards.a: It swaps the side. Just below 1 becomes just above 1, and just above 1 becomes just below 1 — which is why finding the limit first and flooring that is the careless move these questions punish.

flashcards.q: What is the limit of the natural log of 1 plus ax, over x, as x approaches 0?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{\ln(1+ax)}{x} = a$$Just a, the coefficient of x inside the bracket. The formula needs the same quantity inside and below, and forcing that a into the denominator is what leaves it as the answer.

flashcards.q: A difference of two logs over x — merge them or split them?
flashcards.a: Split the fraction into two fractions. Each piece is then the standard form, giving a and minus b, so the answer drops out as a plus b.

flashcards.q: The base of the logarithm is not e. What is the first line of working?
flashcards.a: $$\log_b a = \frac{\ln a}{\ln b}$$Base changing: the natural log of the input over the natural log of the base. Input on top, base below — so a base 3 log leaves a clean 1 over the natural log of 3 standing outside.

flashcards.q: Does a logarithm sitting in the denominator need base changing?
flashcards.a: No. Take the reciprocal instead and the base and the input trade places.

flashcards.q: The logarithm shows no 1 inside it anywhere. What are the two routes?
flashcards.a: Either pull the constant out as a sum of logs, so each piece reads 1 plus something; or squeeze everything into one log and write the inside as 1 plus the inside minus 1. The second route never fails.

flashcards.q: What is cosine 2x minus 1, and why does the order matter?
flashcards.a: $$\cos 2x - 1 = -2\sin^2 x$$Minus twice the sine squared of x. The standard identity is written the other way round, so that minus is the entire reason this limit comes out negative.

flashcards.q: Bringing the log remainder into the denominator — what must stay balanced?
flashcards.a: Whatever you put below must be multiplied back on top. You may only multiply and divide by that bracket, never drop it in for free. And check first that the bracket itself approaches 0.

flashcards.q: What is the first move the moment 1 minus cosine of anything appears?
flashcards.a: $$1 - \cos\theta = 2\sin^{2}\frac{\theta}{2}$$Replace it with twice the sine squared of half the angle. That halving is where the extra constants come from, so track the angle rather than copying a remembered coefficient.

flashcards.q: Why is the log of 1 plus x squared over 3, divided by x squared, not equal to 1?
flashcards.a: Because the value 1 needs you to divide by the exact quantity inside the bracket. Dividing by x squared leaves the coefficient behind, so the value is 1 over 3.

flashcards.q: Both terms of a difference run to infinity. What form is that, and what may you do with it?
flashcards.a: $$\infty - \infty$$An infinity minus infinity form, which is indeterminate: no cancelling and no conclusion. Rewrite the expression into one piece first, then substitute.

flashcards.q: What is the single rule this trap teaches?
flashcards.a: Substitute the limiting value into the whole expression at once. The moment you substitute in one factor and leave another waiting, the question has been changed.

flashcards.q: How is a coefficient in front of a logarithm cleared before merging two logs?
flashcards.a: $$a\ln(1+h) = \ln(1+h)^{a}$$Pull it inside as a power. The difference of the two logs then becomes the log of a quotient, which is the only way past the infinity minus infinity trap.

flashcards.q: Where does the minus sign in this limit come from?
flashcards.a: From the add-one-subtract-one step. The numerator is smaller than the denominator, so the leftover term is negative, and that single sign is the difference between plus 1 and the correct minus 1.

flashcards.q: Why is the limit of e to the 3x, minus 1, over x not equal to 1?
flashcards.a: Because the value 1 needs the power and the denominator to be the same quantity. Make 3x appear below, and the leftover reciprocal leaves 3. Keep the sign too — a power of minus 5x gives minus 5.

flashcards.q: What is the limit of a to the x times b to the x, minus a to the x, minus b to the x, plus 1, all over x squared?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{a^{x}b^{x} - a^{x} - b^{x} + 1}{x^{2}} = \ln a \cdot \ln b$$The product of the two logs. The numerator factorises into two brackets, each a standard exponential limit, and brackets that multiply give logs that multiply — not logs that add.

flashcards.q: In a product question, how do you decide what goes underneath each block?
flashcards.a: Ask each block what it needs below it and give it exactly that, writing the same thing on top to keep the balance. Every block then becomes 1 and only an easy ratio survives.

flashcards.q: Both terms in the numerator are exponentials. What is the first step?
flashcards.a: $$e^{\alpha x} - e^{\beta x} = e^{\beta x}\left(e^{(\alpha - \beta)x} - 1\right)$$Take the smaller exponential common, so what is left inside the bracket is an exponential minus 1 — the only shape the standard limit recognises.

flashcards.q: The constant e has been taken common. What must not happen to it?
flashcards.a: It must not be dropped. It sits outside the whole limit and multiplies the final value.

flashcards.q: State the method for a 1 to the power infinity limit.
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x\to a} f(x)^{g(x)} = e^{\lambda}, \quad \lambda = \lim_{x\to a}\big(f(x)-1\big)\,g(x)$$The limit is e to the lambda, where lambda is the limit of base minus 1, times the power. Use it only after checking separately that the base goes to 1 and the power goes to infinity.

flashcards.q: Lambda has come out as a number. Is that the answer?
flashcards.a: No. Lambda is only the exponent, and leaving it as the answer loses the mark. Write the e before you even begin computing lambda, so it cannot be forgotten.

flashcards.q: The base is a rational function. What does base minus 1 collapse to?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{x+3}{x+1} - 1 = \frac{2}{x+1}$$A small numerator over the same denominator, once the LCM is taken. Multiply that by the power and an ordinary infinity over infinity limit is all that is left.

flashcards.q: What sort of limit survives after base minus 1 is multiplied by the power?
flashcards.a: A plain infinity over infinity, usually with the same degree above and below, so read off the coefficients of the highest power. That ratio is lambda, and nothing new is needed.

flashcards.q: Name the tool for the infinity over infinity form.
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{a_n x^n + \cdots}{b_m x^m + \cdots} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{divide numerator and denominator by } x^{\max(n,m)}$$Divide the numerator and the denominator by the biggest infinity in the expression — not by whichever power you happen to read first, or the limit blows up or collapses to 0.

flashcards.q: How is the technique for an indeterminate form chosen?
flashcards.a: Name the form before any algebra. 0/0 means factorise or rationalise; infinity over infinity means divide by the biggest infinity; infinity minus infinity means take the LCM; 1 to the power infinity means the lambda formula; and 0 times infinity gets pushed down into one of the first two.

flashcards.q: Which of the six expansions hold for every real x, and which are restricted?
flashcards.a: Sine, cosine and e to the x hold for every real x. Tangent needs x between minus pi over 2 and pi over 2, the log of 1 plus x needs x greater than minus 1 and at most 1, and the binomial needs x between minus 1 and 1.

flashcards.q: How do you get the expansion of the sine of 2x?
flashcards.a: $$\sin 2x = 2x - \frac{(2x)^{3}}{3!} + \frac{(2x)^{5}}{5!} - \cdots = 2x - \frac{4x^{3}}{3} + \frac{4x^{5}}{15} - \cdots$$Replace x by 2x on both sides of the standard series, keeping the whole 2x in a bracket before the power is applied, so the cube lands on the number as well as on x.

flashcards.q: Which two questions rebuild any of these series from scratch?
flashcards.a: Is the function odd or even, which fixes whether only odd or only even powers survive; and what is its value at 0, which fixes the first term. Then fill in the alternating signs and the factorials.

flashcards.q: After expanding, how is the outcome of the limit decided?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{a x^{m} + \cdots}{\alpha x^{n} + \cdots} = \begin{cases} a/\alpha & m = n \\ 0 & m > n \\ \text{undefined} & m < n \end{cases}$$Compare the minimum power of x on top with the one below. Equal powers give the ratio of those two coefficients, a bigger power on top gives 0, and a smaller power on top means there is no finite value.

flashcards.q: How far should an expansion be written out?
flashcards.a: Only until the minimum power shows up on both the top and the bottom. The terms above it do no work at all — their coefficients could be anything and the answer would not change.

flashcards.q: What is the shortcut for a function sitting over a power of x?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{f(x)}{x^n} = \text{coefficient of } x^n \text{ in the expansion of } f(x)$$The limit is simply the coefficient of that power in the expansion of the function. Read the denominator's power first, then write only that one term of the series.

flashcards.q: The denominator reads x squared times sine x. What power is that really?
flashcards.a: x cubed. Split it as x cubed times sine x over x, where the bracket goes to 1, so the coefficient to hunt for is the one on x cubed.

flashcards.q: The lowest surviving power on top is higher than the power below. What is the limit?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to 0} \frac{a_m x^m + a_{m+1} x^{m+1} + \cdots}{b_n x^n + \cdots} = 0 \quad (m > n)$$0, including the case where the matching coefficient turned out to be zero. A zero coefficient is information, not an error — it simply moves the minimum power up by one.

flashcards.q: Your expansion leaves a lower power on top than the denominator carries. What does that tell you?
flashcards.a: That no finite limit exists, which no paper sets. So those low powers were meant to cancel, and it is the expansion that needs rechecking, not the question.

flashcards.q: How is the sine of bx expanded?
flashcards.a: $$\sin(bx) = bx - \frac{b^{3}x^{3}}{3!} + \cdots$$Replace x by bx everywhere in the standard series, so the cube comes along with it and the third term carries b cubed.

flashcards.q: Three unknowns and a finite limit. Where do the three equations come from?
flashcards.a: Every power below the denominator's power must have coefficient 0, and the coefficient of the matching power equals the given limit. If the given limit is 0, that matching coefficient is 0 as well.

flashcards.q: Where does the slip happen in a binomial expansion limit?
flashcards.a: In the bracket's x part. With 2x inside, the x squared term carries 2x all squared, so that 4 has to appear in the answer. And for a fractional index below 1, n minus 1 comes out negative, which is why these answers are usually negative.

flashcards.q: What beats the natural log of x as x runs to infinity?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to \infty} \frac{\ln x}{x^{n}} = 0 \quad (n > 0)$$Any positive power of x. The log over that power goes to 0.

flashcards.q: Which limits force you to differentiate rather than expand?
flashcards.a: Ones where cancelling the common factor would need two long divisions, and ones containing a plain log of x — you have the expansion of the log of 1 plus x, not of the log of x.

flashcards.q: What has to be written beside the question before you differentiate?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to a} \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \lim_{x \to a} \frac{f'(x)}{g'(x)}$$The form. Substitute the value first and note the 0/0 or the infinity over infinity next to the question — that scribble is the licence to differentiate, top alone and bottom alone, never as a quotient.

flashcards.q: The question could be expanded, but the instruction is to differentiate. What do you do?
flashcards.a: Use the method you were asked for, and keep the expansion answer only as a check on yourself. A right method with a wrong number is still a wrong answer.

flashcards.q: Which standard limit tells you to stop differentiating?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{e^{x}-1}{x}=1$$The exponential one: e to the x, minus 1, over x, going to 1. The moment a standard limit appears, stop applying the rule and read the value off.

flashcards.q: In a limit as alpha approaches beta, which letter is the variable?
flashcards.a: The one the arrow starts from, alpha. Whatever the arrow points to is a constant, so you differentiate with respect to alpha only.

flashcards.q: Write the full condition for continuity at x = a.
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = f(a)$$The left-hand limit, the right-hand limit and f(a) must all be equal, and all three must be finite. If one side limit blows up, the point is discontinuous and no further checking is needed.

flashcards.q: In a piecewise function, which piece gives the left-hand limit at a point?
flashcards.a: $$f(a^-) = \lim_{x \to a^-} f(x), \quad f(a^+) = \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x)$$The piece that is valid just below the point. Choose the piece by the side you are standing on first, write it down, and only then substitute.

flashcards.q: How is f(a) found for a piecewise function?
flashcards.a: Find the line of the definition that covers the point itself and substitute. Nothing clever is needed — that number is f(a).

flashcards.q: What is e to the minus infinity?
flashcards.a: $$e^{-\infty} = \frac{1}{e^{\infty}} = \frac{1}{\infty} \to 0, \qquad e^{+\infty} \to \infty$$1 over e to the infinity, that is 1 over something blowing up, so it goes to 0. The exponential is never negative — a minus in the power sends it to 0, not to minus infinity.

flashcards.q: Why must 1 over x never be given a two-sided limit at 0?
flashcards.a: Because the two sides behave in opposite ways: it runs to plus infinity from the right and to minus infinity from the left. Write the two one-sided limits separately and only then compare.

flashcards.q: State the definition of the greatest integer function, and what it does at an integer.
flashcards.a: $$[x] = n \quad \text{for } n \le x < n+1,\ n \in \mathbb{Z}$$It equals n for every x from n up to but not including n plus 1. At an integer it jumps, so the left side sits one step lower than the right side.

flashcards.q: A continuity question offers no options and asks for k. What do you set up?
flashcards.a: The equation left-hand limit equals right-hand limit equals f(a). That equation hands you k, whereas substitution on its own only gives f(a).

flashcards.q: What is the greatest integer of x plus the greatest integer of minus x?
flashcards.a: $$[x]+[-x]=\begin{cases}0, & x\in\mathbb{Z}\\ -1, & x\notin\mathbb{Z}\end{cases}$$0 when x is an integer, and minus 1 otherwise. So the function breaks at every integer and is continuous everywhere between them.

flashcards.q: Is 0 over infinity an indeterminate form?
flashcards.a: No, it is determinate: small divided by huge is 0. Write the answer and move to the other side of the point — no differentiation rule is needed.

flashcards.q: How do you handle a ratio of cotangents in a limit at 0?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{\cot 4x}{\cot 2x}=\frac{\tan 2x}{\tan 4x}$$Flip it into a ratio of tangents, which swaps the angles, so the limit is the reciprocal ratio of the two angles.

flashcards.q: The formula excludes pi over 4, yet f is continuous on an open interval containing it. What is f at pi over 4?
flashcards.a: It is forced to equal the limit there. At an interior point of an interval on which the function is continuous, the value has no freedom at all.

flashcards.q: Where can a piecewise function break?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to c^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to c^+} f(x) = f(c)$$Only at the points where its definition changes. Apply the three-way test at those joints alone, because inside each piece the formula is a standard continuous function.

flashcards.q: One of the two change points has been cleared. Is the work finished?
flashcards.a: No. Each joint needs its own equation — continuity at one joint says nothing at all about the other.

flashcards.q: How do you rewrite the greatest integer of x times x squared on an interval?
flashcards.a: $$f(x)=\begin{cases}-2x^{2}, & -2\le x<-1\\ -x^{2}, & -1\le x<0\\ 0, & 0\le x<1\\ 1, & x=1\end{cases}$$On each unit interval the greatest integer is a fixed number, so write that number in front of x squared. The bracket then leaves your working and every piece is an ordinary polynomial.

flashcards.q: The definition changes at a point. Is that enough to call it discontinuous?
flashcards.a: No — a change of definition is a suspect, not a verdict. Where the left piece, the right piece and the value all give the same number, the point is continuous.

flashcards.q: What is checked at the left end point of the domain?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = f(a)$$Right-continuity only: the right-hand limit must equal the value there. The other side is not in the domain, so it is never tested.

flashcards.q: Why can an end point never be the hard case?
flashcards.a: Because only one side of it lies in the domain, so it is one comparison instead of two. Whatever the curve does outside the domain carries no information.

flashcards.q: Substitution gives a clean finite value. What is the limit?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = f(a)$$That value. A determinate form needs no method at all — only 0/0 or infinity over infinity earns one.

flashcards.q: Where does the limit-equals-value shortcut break down?
flashcards.a: In a piecewise function. There the value of the function and a one-sided limit can disagree, and that disagreement is exactly where discontinuity comes from.

flashcards.q: The one-sided limits disagree. Can one redefinition repair the point?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) \neq \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x)$$No. The limit does not exist, so the discontinuity is irremovable however many patches are tried. You may rewrite f at that single point only — touching the formula creates a new function.

flashcards.q: The limit exists but the value at that point is not given at all. What is this called?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = L \ \text{exists}, \quad f(a) \ \text{not defined}$$A missing point discontinuity, one of the two removable sub-types. On the graph there is only the hollow circle and no dark circle at that x.

flashcards.q: How are the two removable sub-types told apart on a graph?
flashcards.a: Count the circles at that point. The hollow circle is the limit and the dark circle is the value, so two circles mean isolated point, and a hollow circle alone means missing point.

flashcards.q: The sine of 1 over x stays bounded near 0. Does its limit exist there?
flashcards.a: $$-1 \le \sin\left(\frac{1}{x}\right) \le 1 \ \text{for all} \ x \neq 0$$No. Bounded is not the same as convergent — the function oscillates instead of settling, so the limit does not exist and the discontinuity is essential.

flashcards.q: Count the limits: how do the three families differ?
flashcards.a: A removable type gives one number, with only the value wrong or missing. A jump gives two different numbers. An essential one gives no number at all.

flashcards.q: What is the limit of the log of 1 minus bx, over x, as x approaches 0?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x\to 0}\frac{\ln(1-bx)}{x}=-b$$Minus b. The limit is the whole coefficient of x inside the log, sign included.

flashcards.q: The working has reached m squared equals 40. What is easy to lose?
flashcards.a: The negative root. A square gives both signs, so both values stand unless the question itself restricts m.

flashcards.q: Where do you hunt for the breaks of a greatest integer of a function?
flashcards.a: $$g(x) \in \mathbb{Z} \;\Rightarrow\; \lfloor g(x) \rfloor \text{ may jump at that } x$$At the x values where the output of the inside function hits a whole number — not at integer values of x. The bracket cares about the output, never the input.

flashcards.q: What is the first move on a greatest-integer-of-a-quadratic question?
flashcards.a: Graph the quadratic on the given interval. The graph hands you the crossings of the integer levels, and every root found must then be checked against that interval before it is counted.

flashcards.q: How is the vertex of a quadratic found without a table of points?
flashcards.a: $$y_v = -\frac{D}{4a}, \quad D = b^2 - 4ac$$The x coordinate is minus b over 2a and the y coordinate is minus the discriminant over 4a. Those two numbers, plus the two end values, fix the whole graph.

flashcards.q: The two end values came out equal. Is that a coincidence?
flashcards.a: No. Both ends are the same distance from the vertex line, so their heights must match. If they come out different, the arithmetic needs rechecking.

flashcards.q: When does the greatest integer of a value equal n?
flashcards.a: $$[y]=n \iff n \le y < n+1$$When the value reaches n but stays short of n plus 1. That single rule builds every flat step of the staircase.

flashcards.q: Why does the vertex of this curve sit on the step of height 2?
flashcards.a: Because the lowest value, 11 over 4, is 2.75, whose greatest integer is 2. That step is also the proof that the curve never touched 2 exactly, which is why both of its ends are hollow.

flashcards.q: The paper wants the sum of two jump points that come from the same level. What do you write?
flashcards.a: $$\alpha + \beta = -\frac{b}{a}$$Minus b over a, the sum of the roots of that one quadratic. Solving for the roots and adding them back is wasted time.

flashcards.q: Before using the sum of roots, what has to be confirmed?
flashcards.a: That both roots lie inside the given interval. And the end points of the interval must be counted too, since the curve sits exactly on an integer level there.

flashcards.q: Which step does an exact integer belong to?
flashcards.a: $$[x] = 5 \text{ at } x = 5$$The new one. At 5 the greatest integer is 5, not 4 — the left integer of a step is included and the right one is never reached.

flashcards.q: Why is a greatest-integer question really a range question?
flashcards.a: Because the break points are the integers the inside value passes through. Find what the expression ranges over, read each flat piece as integer included and next integer excluded, and the graph draws itself.

flashcards.q: Which number decides how many integer levels the curve can touch?
flashcards.a: $$x_{\text{vertex}} = -\frac{b}{2a}, \qquad f_{\min} = c - \frac{b^2}{4a}$$The lowest value, taken from the vertex. The two end values are not enough, because a parabola can sit far below both of them.

flashcards.q: If the minimum value had been lower, what would change?
flashcards.a: More integer levels would fall inside the range, so there would be more break points to collect. The method itself does not change: find the range, then the integers inside it.

flashcards.q: How is a one-sided limit of a composite computed?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x\to a^+} f(g(x)) = f\!\left(g(a^+)\right), \qquad \lim_{x\to a^-} f(g(x)) = f\!\left(g(a^-)\right)$$Take the one-sided value of the inner function first, then feed that into the outer function. The composite is never built as a new piecewise function.

flashcards.q: Why keep the inner values as slightly bigger and slightly smaller rather than as plain numbers?
flashcards.a: Because the outer function reads that sign to choose its branch, and dropping it picks the wrong definition. The final answer, though, is always a clean number — the plus or minus belongs to inputs only.

flashcards.q: State the signum function.
flashcards.a: $$\operatorname{sgn}(x)=\begin{cases}+1, & x>0\\ 0, & x=0\\ -1, & x<0\end{cases}$$Plus 1 for a positive input, minus 1 for a negative one, and 0 at exactly zero. Only the sign of the input matters, never its size.

flashcards.q: The inner function jumps at the point. Must the composite jump too?
flashcards.a: No. If both sides land strictly on the same side of zero, the signum flattens them to the same value and the composite is continuous. The jump survives only if the two sides straddle zero, or if one of them is exactly zero.

flashcards.q: The denominator vanishes at a point while the numerator does not. What follows?
flashcards.a: $$f(x)=\frac{g(x)}{h(x)},\; h(a)=0,\; g(a)\neq 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \lim_{x\to a} f(x)=\pm\infty$$The limit is infinite, so that point is outside the domain and the function is discontinuous there. No one-sided limits are needed.

flashcards.q: Both one-sided limits of 1 over x squared at 0 are plus infinity. Is it continuous there?
flashcards.a: No. Infinity is not a value — the common limit must be finite and equal to the value of the function, which does not even exist at that point.

flashcards.q: Where is the composite discontinuous once it has been simplified?
flashcards.a: $$f(x) = \frac{x+1}{x-1},\quad g(x) = \frac{1}{x-2} \;\Rightarrow\; (f \circ g)(x) = \frac{x-1}{3-x}$$At the zeros of the simplified denominator, and also at every point where the inner function blows up. Cancelling changes the expression, never the domain.

flashcards.q: Which list of bad points do you write first?
flashcards.a: The bad points of the inner function, in the margin, before any algebra. Simplification can cancel a factor, but it can never give back a point the domain never had.

flashcards.q: Two checks settle a function composed with itself. What are they?
flashcards.a: $$f(f(x)) = \cfrac{1}{1 - \cfrac{1}{1-x}} = \frac{x-1}{x}$$Where the inner copy dies, and where the simplified expression dies. Both are points of discontinuity, and the first is the one the paper is really testing.

flashcards.q: What is the common slip when substituting a function into itself?
flashcards.a: Replacing x by only part of the inner output. The entire inner output goes into the slot, so write the rule with the word input in the slot and then paste the whole inner expression in.

flashcards.q: Write the slope of the chord joining a point and its neighbour h away.
flashcards.a: $$m_{AB} = \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{(a+h) - a} = \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}$$The change in the function value divided by h, because the denominator always collapses to h. Only the numerator needs any work.

flashcards.q: Why not put h equal to 0 in the slope of the chord?
flashcards.a: Because then the two points coincide and there is no chord at all. h only tends to 0, so the neighbour comes as close as you like but stays a separate point. And the function cannot be split — the whole of the shifted input goes inside it.

flashcards.q: State the first principle at a point, and say what it means geometrically.
flashcards.a: $$f'(a) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(a+h) - f(a)}{h}$$It is the limit of the change in the function over h as h goes to 0, and that limit is the slope of the tangent at the point.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between the derivative as a rule and the derivative at a point?
flashcards.a: The rule holds for the whole function; the value at a point is the actual slope of the tangent there. The slope changes from point to point.

flashcards.q: How many formulas do you actually need for the two one-sided derivatives?
flashcards.a: One. Remember the right-hand one and replace h by minus h everywhere to get the left-hand one, the denominator included. h stays positive in both — the direction is carried by the minus sign you write.

flashcards.q: How many tangents can be drawn at a point where a graph is differentiable?
flashcards.a: Exactly one — unique just means one. A sharp corner lets two be drawn, so it is non-differentiable there, and a break in the graph is the other way differentiability fails.

flashcards.q: State the complete test for differentiability at a point.
flashcards.a: $$f \text{ differentiable at } x=a \iff f \text{ continuous at } x=a \ \text{ and } \ f'(a^{+}) = f'(a^{-})$$Continuity at that point, and the right-hand derivative equal to the left-hand derivative. Check continuity first: if it fails, write non-differentiable and stop.

flashcards.q: When is the equal-slopes condition worth checking?
flashcards.a: $$f'(a^{+}) = f'(a^{-})$$Only after continuity at the point has been confirmed. Equal one-sided derivatives cannot rescue a broken graph, because at a break two tangents exist even when they are parallel.

flashcards.q: Must a discontinuous graph have unequal one-sided derivatives?
flashcards.a: No. A broken graph can easily have two parallel tangents, so the equality of the slopes says nothing at all about the break.

flashcards.q: How is the right-hand derivative obtained without writing a limit?
flashcards.a: $$f'(a^{+}) = \left[\frac{d}{dx}\,f_{\,x>a}(x)\right]_{x=a}$$Differentiate the piece valid to the right of the point, then substitute the point into that derivative. The standard formulas are those limits, already solved.

flashcards.q: Both pieces gave the same value at the point. Does that settle differentiability?
flashcards.a: No, it only proves continuity. The two slopes can still differ, and that is exactly the sharp corner case.

flashcards.q: Which piece gives the left-hand derivative at the join?
flashcards.a: $$f'(1^{-})=\left[\frac{d}{dx}\left(2x^{2}+x+6\right)\right]_{x=1}$$The one valid below the point. Differentiate it while x is still there and substitute the point only at the last step.

flashcards.q: Both the value and the slope matched at the join. What does that mean?
flashcards.a: Value first, slope second: matching values give continuity, and matching slopes then give differentiability, so the join is smooth.

flashcards.q: A jump has been found at the point. What else needs doing?
flashcards.a: $$f \text{ discontinuous at } x=a \;\Longrightarrow\; f \text{ not differentiable at } x=a$$Nothing. The function is non-differentiable there, and the one-sided derivatives cannot change that.

flashcards.q: One constant was changed and the answer flipped. What did not change?
flashcards.a: The two derivatives — they stay exactly as they were. Only continuity changed, which is why continuity is checked first.

flashcards.q: What is step two of the differentiability test, and when is it reached?
flashcards.a: $$f'(a^-) = f'(a^+)$$Equal one-sided derivatives, checked only once continuity has passed. The two steps together say the same thing as one unique tangent at the point.

flashcards.q: Of the three cases set side by side, what does the broken one with equal slopes show?
flashcards.a: That a break is about the value, not the slope, so the two pieces can easily have the same slope and the point is still non-differentiable.

flashcards.q: At a joining point, what is the fixed order of work?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to a^-} f(x) = \lim_{x \to a^+} f(x) = f(a)$$Value first, slope second. Put the number into both pieces and match the values, then differentiate both pieces and match the slopes. If the values disagree, stop there.

flashcards.q: The pieces are neat polynomials. Can continuity be assumed?
flashcards.a: No. Polynomials are continuous on their own, but the two pieces can still disagree at the joining point, and only the matched values prove otherwise.

flashcards.q: Two unknown constants at a joining point. How many equations, and where from?
flashcards.a: $$f'(a^-) = f'(a^+)$$Exactly two: one from continuity and one from the equality of the one-sided derivatives. If only one equation has been written, the continuity line has been missed.

flashcards.q: Why differentiate before substituting the joining point?
flashcards.a: Because substituting first kills the x and the relation is lost. Differentiate the piece as it stands, then put the point into the derivative.

flashcards.q: The two one-sided limits disagree. Do you still compute the derivatives?
flashcards.a: $$f \text{ discontinuous at } c \Rightarrow f \text{ not differentiable at } c$$No. Stop at the limits — discontinuous means non-differentiable, so write that and move to the next question.

flashcards.q: Which of the two relations usually hands you a constant for free?
flashcards.a: The derivative one. Matching the derivatives of the two pieces at the junction normally drops one constant out at once, and the continuity relation then gives the other.

flashcards.q: Where is a modulus split, and what does the question become afterwards?
flashcards.a: At the point where the inside becomes zero. From that line on it is the ordinary piecewise question you have already solved, and below that point the modulus flips the sign of the inside.

flashcards.q: Which kind of question forces the one-sided derivative definitions?
flashcards.a: $$f'(a^-)=\lim_{h\to 0^+}\frac{f(a-h)-f(a)}{-h},\qquad f'(a^+)=\lim_{h\to 0^+}\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$$The third kind, where a single formula cannot be differentiated by the usual rules at the point. In the other two you differentiate each piece and match them at the breakpoint.

flashcards.q: Name the three kinds of continuity and differentiability question.
flashcards.a: The pieces are given to you; you have to make the pieces yourself, as with a modulus or a greatest integer; or you must go back to the one-sided derivative definition. The second collapses into the first the moment the pieces are written down.

flashcards.q: What is the fractional part, and why is it harmless?
flashcards.a: $$\{x\} = x - [x]$$It is x minus the greatest integer of x. Swap it in at once: between two integers the bracket is only a constant, so it never fights back when you differentiate.

flashcards.q: A point has been found non-differentiable. Is the work finished?
flashcards.a: Not necessarily. A non-differentiable point still has a right-hand and a left-hand derivative — find both, and they simply will not match.

flashcards.q: What can be done with a modulus sitting inside a cosine?
flashcards.a: $$\cos|x| = \cos x \quad \text{for all } x$$It can be dropped straight away, because the cosine is even. A modulus inside a sine cannot be: the sine is odd, so that one has to be split.

flashcards.q: In these modulus-plus-smooth-function examples, which part carries the break?
flashcards.a: The modulus part. The smooth piece behaves well at the point while the modulus flips sign, which is why the two answers come out equal in size and opposite in sign.

flashcards.q: A modulus vanishes at a point. Which test settles differentiability there?
flashcards.a: $$f'(c^-) = f'(c^+) \iff f \text{ is differentiable at } x=c$$Whether the two one-sided derivatives agree. A zero of the inside is only a suspect point, never a verdict on its own.

flashcards.q: Why does one zero of the modulus survive and the other not?
flashcards.a: Count the power of the vanishing factor. Where that factor appears twice, every term of the derivative still carries it and both sides collapse to 0. Where it appears once, nothing cancels and a corner is left.

flashcards.q: What is the greatest integer just to the left of an integer?
flashcards.a: $$\lfloor x \rfloor = n-1 \quad \text{for } n-1 \le x < n$$One less than that integer. So on the left the function becomes that smaller constant times x squared, while on the right it is the integer itself times x squared.

flashcards.q: Why is the origin the one integer where this function survives?
flashcards.a: Because the jump in the bracket is multiplied by x squared, and only there is the multiplier itself zero. The jump is wiped out, so the point is both continuous and differentiable.

flashcards.q: What are the two swaps that clear a greatest-integer and fractional-part question?
flashcards.a: $$\lfloor x \rfloor = n \quad \text{for } n \le x < n+1$$Fix the interval first, then put the constant in for the greatest integer and x minus that constant in for the fractional part. After those two swaps you are holding an ordinary polynomial.

flashcards.q: What changes the moment an integer is crossed?
flashcards.a: The constant. Just below 1 you are inside the stretch from 0 to 1, so the greatest integer is 0 and the fractional part is x itself. Write the interval down before substituting, and settle continuity before any derivative.

flashcards.q: Continuous times discontinuous — when is the product still continuous?
flashcards.a: $$\lim_{x \to a} f(x) = 0 \;\Rightarrow\; \lim_{x \to a^{-}} f(x)g(x) = 0 = \lim_{x \to a^{+}} f(x)g(x)$$When the limit of the continuous factor is 0. Zero times either of the other function's two values gives 0 both times, so the jump vanishes; any non-zero limit keeps the two values apart.

flashcards.q: A differentiable function plus a non-differentiable one — what follows?
flashcards.a: $$g \text{ differentiable},\; h \text{ not} \;\Rightarrow\; g \pm h \text{ not differentiable}$$The sum is not differentiable, which rejects an option in one line. There is no matching rule the other way: two non-differentiable functions can add to a differentiable one, because two corners can cancel.

flashcards.q: Where can a modulus term break differentiability?
flashcards.a: Only where the inside equals 0. Factorise, list those points and check nothing else — and if that zero is also a zero of the factor multiplying the modulus, a square forms and the point survives.

flashcards.q: Which two differentiation facts does this whole category need?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dh}\,f\big(g(h)\big) = f'\big(g(h)\big)\cdot g'(h), \qquad \frac{d}{dh}\,f(a) = 0$$The chain rule on the moving part, and zero for the frozen part: a bracket holding only the fixed value is just a number, so its derivative is 0.

flashcards.q: The limit looks like a derivative. Should you reach for the definition?
flashcards.a: Not while it is a plain 0/0 that can be differentiated. Substitute the limiting value first to confirm the form — that substitution also shows which values of the function and its derivative the question is secretly asking for.

flashcards.q: Differentiating the function of a bracket such as 5 minus t — what must be carried?
flashcards.a: $$\frac{d}{dt}\,f(5-t) = -f'(5-t)$$The derivative of the bracket, which is minus 1 here. That single minus sign is what makes the two terms add instead of cancelling.

flashcards.q: In the difference quotient, what is the value of the function at the fixed point?
flashcards.a: A constant like any other number, so its derivative is 0. Writing the derivative of the function there instead is the one mistake made in this type.

flashcards.q: State the test for differentiability in terms of the two one-sided definitions.
flashcards.a: $$f'(a^{-}) = f'(a^{+}) = \text{finite} \iff f \text{ is differentiable at } x = a$$The left-hand derivative and the right-hand derivative must be equal, and both must be finite.

flashcards.q: If the standard formulas always work, why learn the definition?
flashcards.a: Because every formula is the definition already evaluated, and when the standard form breaks down at a point the definition has to be run by hand. Note the step size: stepping to a minus h makes the denominator minus h.

flashcards.q: Why does a vanishing factor times the sine of 1 over x go to 0?
flashcards.a: $$-1 \le \sin\frac{1}{x} \le 1, \qquad -1 \le \cos\frac{1}{x} \le 1$$Because the sine never leaves the band from minus 1 to plus 1, however wildly it oscillates. Something going to 0, times a bounded factor, has limit 0.

flashcards.q: The direct derivative has no value at the point. Does that settle differentiability?
flashcards.a: No. That formula is valid only away from the point, so its failure proves nothing. Write the one-sided derivatives from the definition instead, remembering to subtract the given value at the point.

flashcards.q: Why does the squared version have a derivative at the origin?
flashcards.a: $$f(x)=\begin{cases}x^{2}\sin\frac{1}{x}, & x\neq 0\\ 0, & x=0\end{cases}\;\Rightarrow\; f'(0)=\lim_{h\to 0}h\sin\frac{1}{h}=0$$Because one factor of h survives in the difference quotient, and that vanishing factor squeezes the oscillation to 0. Without the square the quotient is left as the sine of 1 over h, which has no limit.

flashcards.q: Continuity has been established at the origin. What does that give you about the derivative?
flashcards.a: Nothing. Continuity is the weaker condition, and this function is the clean counter-example: continuous there with no derivative. Test the derivative separately, from the definition.

mistakes.m: Treating 0/0 as a number, or substituting x = 9.9999 to guess the answer.
mistakes.fix: 0/0 is only a signal that work is pending — factorize, rationalize or divide; never plug in a nearby decimal.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Letting x → −∞ directly inside a square root, so the sign of the answer comes out wrong.
mistakes.fix: Always put x = −t so t → +∞, because √t² = t only for positive t; (x+5)/√(2x²+1) then gives −1/√2, not +1/√2.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Using sin x/x = 1 wherever a sine appears.
mistakes.fix: It is 1 only when the angle itself → 0; at x → π/2 the value of sin x/x is simply 2/π. Reshape the problem so the angle tends to 0 before using the formula.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Splitting a limit into two parts while a part is still indeterminate.
mistakes.fix: Substitute the limiting value into the whole expression at once; splitting ln(1+2h)/h² − 2ln(1+h)/h² makes a fake ∞ − ∞ and a fake answer of 0. Split only when each piece is already finite.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Applying ln(1+u)/u → 1 to a log that is not to base e.
mistakes.fix: Convert first with log_b a = ln a / ln b; a base-3 log leaves an extra 1/ln 3 in the answer.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Reading the angle in degrees as if it were radians.
mistakes.fix: Every trig limit formula is in radians, so x degrees = πx/180; that is why the answer becomes π/180 and not 1.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Computing LHD and RHD without checking continuity, then calling the function differentiable because they matched.
mistakes.fix: Check LHL = RHL = f(a) first; a discontinuous point is non-differentiable even when both derivatives come out equal.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
For f(g(x)), reporting only the points where the simplified expression breaks.
mistakes.fix: Add every point where the inner function itself blows up — there the whole calculation is meaningless, so it is a point of discontinuity too.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Differentiating f(5 − t) with respect to t and forgetting the inner −1.
mistakes.fix: Chain rule gives −f'(5 − t), so [f(5+t) − f(5−t)]/2t → f'(5), not 0.

mistakes.m: ▶ where this comes up in the lecture
Guessing where a greatest-integer function breaks instead of drawing it.
mistakes.fix: Graph the inside function on the given interval first; only the integer levels it actually crosses, plus the interval ends, can be points of discontinuity.
